teaser: The most famous pose of Henry VIII comes from a wall that burned down in 1698.
review_notes:
IMAGE/METADATA MISMATCH: the image is not the small Thyssen-Bornemisza panel portrait of Henry VIII. It is George Vertue's engraving (1737) after Remigius van Leemput's 1667 copy of Holbein's lost Whitehall mural of 1537 (Henry VII, Elizabeth of York, Henry VIII, Jane Seymour). The lesson is written about the image shown and mentions the Thyssen panel only in the last block.
Vertue's print dated 1737; lesson says 'in the 1700s'.
Henry's jousting accident of January 1536, 'unconscious for two hours': from a contemporary ambassador's report, sometimes doubted.
Cartoon for the left half in the National Portrait Gallery, London, pricked for transfer; Henry's head in three-quarter view there, frontal in the mural. 'Perhaps at the king's request' is speculation.
Paraphrase of the Latin inscription (father versus son).
Karel van Mander's 1604 report that viewers felt abashed before the mural.
Whitehall fire: January 1698.
Thyssen panel: about 28 x 20 cm, oil on oak, c. 1537.
Henry aged about 46 in 1537 (born June 1491).
The image is a monochrome print of modest resolution: spots point only at whole figures and clearly legible features.

lesson.text: Four people share this room, and two of them were long dead when it was painted. The older man leaning on the stone block is King Henry VII, who died in 1509. The woman facing him, his queen Elizabeth of York, died in 1503. In front of them stand their son Henry VIII and his third wife, Jane Seymour, very much alive in 1537. Ghosts and the living pose like one family photograph.

There is a second oddity. What you see is a print, not a painting. Hans Holbein, the king's German-born court painter, made this group life size in 1537 on a wall of Whitehall Palace in London, in the king's private rooms. That wall no longer exists. The image survives through copies like this one, engraved in the 1700s by George Vertue.

lesson.title: The royal family
lesson.text: Their names are carved in the band above their heads. Meet them one at a time.

spots.title: The father
spots.text: Henry VII, thin-faced, wrapped in a long fur-lined gown, one arm resting on the block. He won the crown in battle in 1485 and founded the Tudor family line. Holbein never met him.

spots.title: The mother
spots.text: Elizabeth of York in a pointed hood that was out of fashion by 1537. Her marriage joined two rival royal houses and closed the civil wars known as the Wars of the Roses.

spots.title: The wife
spots.text: Jane Seymour, hands folded at her waist. In 1537 she was pregnant with the son Henry had been waiting for through almost thirty years of rule.

spots.title: The king
spots.text: Henry VIII, about 46. Flat feathered cap, jeweled collar, small eyes, square jaw. The other three turn slightly aside. He alone faces whoever walks in.

lesson.text: Did you feel where your eye kept returning? The parents stand higher, on a step, as rank and respect require. Yet the son takes over the picture. Holbein manages it with geometry, and with a body that is closer to a diagram than to anatomy.
Three lines explain how the king wins.

lines.label: The shoulders
lines.text: Padded sleeves and a fur-trimmed coat push his width far beyond any real shoulder. He is nearly as broad as the stone block beside him.

lines.label: The stance
lines.text: Feet planted wide, toes turned out, like a wrestler waiting for an opponent. Earlier kings were shown seated, kneeling or in profile. Nobody had stood like this.

lines.label: Four heads
lines.text: The dead stand higher and further back, the living lower and closer to us. The past retreats, the present steps forward.

lesson.text: That wide stance was a wish more than a fact. In January 1536 Henry was thrown from his horse at a tournament and is said to have lain unconscious for two hours. He never jousted again. A wound on his leg refused to heal, and the athletic prince was turning into a heavy, short-tempered man in pain. Holbein painted the legs the king wanted remembered.

Holbein's full-size working drawing for the left half of the mural still exists, in the National Portrait Gallery in London. Its outlines are pricked with tiny holes: charcoal dust was dabbed through them to transfer the design to the wall.

That drawing holds a clue. In it, Henry's body faces us but his head is turned a little to one side, the usual polite angle for a portrait. On the wall, Holbein swung the face fully to the front. It was a late change, perhaps at the king's request, and it turned a portrait into a confrontation.

Then comes the block in the middle, covered in Latin. Its verses ask a blunt question: who is greater, the father or the son? The father, they say, ended the wars and brought peace. But the son did more: he drove the power of the popes out of England and restored true religion. Henry had broken with Rome only a few years before. The wall is his answer to doubters.
Jane Seymour gave birth to Prince Edward in October 1537 and died twelve days later. The date 1537 is carved in the band above her head, so the mural shows her in the last months of her life.
A solemn, political picture, then, built to impress ambassadors. Still, the image leaves room for one small, warm thing that has nothing to do with crowns. It is down at carpet level.
A fifth guest has slipped into this royal portrait. Find it.

spots.title: The lapdog
spots.text: A small white dog has settled on the train of Jane Seymour's dress. Among Latin verses, stone and jewels, it is the one soft, private note.

lesson.text: The dog, the queen and the kings all went up in smoke. In January 1698 a fire swept through Whitehall Palace and destroyed nearly all of it, Holbein's wall included. Luckily King Charles II had ordered a small painted copy in 1667 from an artist named Remigius van Leemput. The lower inscription on the block in this print records exactly that.
An early biographer of Holbein, writing about sixty years after the painter's death, reported that people who stood before the life-size king felt abashed and overwhelmed.

One painting of Henry by Holbein's own hand does survive from these months: a panel in Madrid's Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum, showing the same face and jeweled costume from the chest up. It is about 28 centimeters high (11 inches), roughly a sheet of office paper. The largest image of the king is ash. The smallest is the one we can still stand in front of.

quiz.question: Which two figures were already dead when the mural was painted in 1537?
options: Henry VII and Elizabeth of York
Jane Seymour and Elizabeth of York
quiz.explanation: Henry's parents had died in 1509 and 1503.

quiz.question: What happened to Holbein's original wall painting?
options: It was destroyed in the Whitehall Palace fire of 1698
Henry VIII had it painted over
quiz.explanation: The fire of 1698 destroyed nearly the whole palace, mural included.

quiz.question: What question do the Latin verses on the stone block ask?
options: Who is greater, the father or the son?
quiz.explanation: The verses compare Henry VII and Henry VIII and favor the son.

quiz.question: Why was Henry's wide, athletic stance flattering in 1537?
options: A jousting accident in 1536 had left him with a bad leg
He had never learned to ride
quiz.explanation: After his 1536 fall he never jousted again and suffered from a leg wound.

quiz.question: How did Holbein change Henry's head between the drawing and the wall?
options: He turned it to face straight out
quiz.explanation: The slightly turned head of the drawing became fully frontal on the wall.

facts.text: The image shown here is an engraving made from a copy of the lost mural.
facts.explanation: George Vertue engraved it in the 1700s after Remigius van Leemput's 1667 painted copy.

facts.text: In the mural, Henry VIII stands on a higher step than his father.
facts.explanation: The parents stand higher and further back, while the son dominates from the front.

facts.text: Holbein's surviving panel of Henry VIII in Madrid is a life-size, full-length portrait.
facts.explanation: It is only about 28 centimeters high and shows him from the chest up.
